title: Why Strategy Alone Doesn't Settle Decisions
author: Kevin Ertell
summary: Sound strategy is necessary but insufficient for good decision-making in organizations. Competing strategic interpretations, disagreements about priorities, and different philosophies about risk all create tension even among leaders aligned on overall strategy. Successful decision-making requires leaders to move beyond strategy alone to examine the underlying values, assumptions, and decision-making principles that guide how they interpret and apply strategy in real situations. Leaders must be explicit about their decision-making frameworks and reasoning to resolve deep disagreements and build alignment.
points: Sound strategy alone cannot settle disagreements because leaders interpret strategy differently based on their values and priorities.
Competing strategic interpretations create real tension between leaders even when they claim alignment on overall strategy and direction.
Decision-making requires examining not just what to do strategically, but the underlying principles that guide how leaders decide.
Leaders must be explicit about their risk philosophies, priority-setting methods, and decision-making frameworks with their teams.
Great leadership means making your decision-making logic transparent so others understand how you arrive at important choices.
Strategy provides direction, but decisions are where direction meets choice under constraints and uncertainty.
When smart people disagree on decisions despite shared strategy, the disagreement is often about underlying values, not facts or data.
quotes: Strategy is the direction, but decisions are where direction meets choice under real constraints and genuine uncertainty.
Two leaders can read the same strategic document and come away with fundamentally different conclusions about what to do.
When smart people disagree on decisions despite shared strategy, the disagreement is often about underlying values, not facts.
Leaders often fail to be explicit about their decision-making principles, leaving teams to guess at their logic.
The best leaders clarify not just their strategy, but how they think about tradeoffs, risk, and priorities.
Decision-making frameworks—your approach to choosing between options—matter as much as your strategic intent.
Most decision disagreements are resolved when leaders surface and align on their underlying decision-making principles.
Strategy aligns direction; decision-making frameworks align how you navigate disagreements along the way.
Without explicit decision-making principles, strategy remains abstract and subject to interpretation.
The clarity leaders need is not about better strategy; it's about being explicit about how they decide.” Archived from Substack (mistere820) on May 2, 2026 by Tim.
